chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad narrated from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from Abu Ayyub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the 'malḥah' (salt mine/field), so he said, 'What is the malḥah?' I said, 'A salty, briny land where water collects and turns into salt.' He said, 'This is a mine, and it contains the khums.' I said, 'And sulfur and petroleum, which are extracted from the earth?' He said, 'This and its like, they contain the khums.'

key_terms.الْخُمُس: The one-fifth tax levied on specific categories of wealth, including minerals
key_terms.الْمَعْدِن: Mine; a source of minerals or extracted resources
key_terms.الْمَلَّحَة: Salt mine or field; a source of salt

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on khums for salt, sulfur, and petroleum extracted from the earth in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that 'malaha' (salt pans) constitute a mineral resource subject to khums, establishing a precedent for extracting wealth from the earth. He explicitly extends this ruling to sulfur and petroleum, demonstrating the juristic principle that all subterranean minerals share this fiscal obligation. This ruling is significant in Shia fiqh for defining the scope of khums beyond agricultural produce to include natural resources.
